title: Style, Documentation & Maintainability 📚
description: Write readable, self‑documenting code with consistent naming, comments, and ShellCheck linting.

slides.title: Why Style Matters 🎨
slides.content:
## Code Is Read More Than Written

A consistent style helps you and others understand the logic quickly.

- Indentation: 2 or 4 spaces, never tabs.
- Line length: keep under 80‑100 characters.
- Use blank lines to separate logical blocks.
- Place `then` on the same line as `if` or on a new line – pick one and stick to it.

quizData.question: Which indentation style is recommended?

options.text: Use tabs because they compress better
Mix tabs and spaces for flexibility
Indentation is not important in Bash

quizData.explanation: Consistent space indentation ensures the code looks the same everywhere.

slides.title: Naming Conventions 🏷️
slides.content:
## Make Names Meaningful

- Variables: `lower_case_with_underscores`.
- Constants: `UPPER_CASE_WITH_UNDERSCORES`.
- Functions: `verb_noun()` e.g., `get_user`, `parse_log`.
- Private functions: `_prefix_with_underscore()`.

Avoid single‑letter names except for loop indices (`i`, `j`). Use `local` for all function‑local variables.

slides.title: Comments: The Why, Not the What 💡
slides.content:
## Document Intent

Explain *why* a piece of code exists, not *what* it does (the what is visible).

- Every script should have a header describing its purpose, author, and usage.
- Every function should have a short comment above it.
- Use `#` for single‑line, `: '...'` for multi‑line block comments.

slides.title: Script Header Template
slides.codeSnippet:
#!/bin/bash
#
# script_name.sh - one‑line description
# Usage: ./script_name.sh [options] <file>
# Author: Your Name
#
set -euo pipefail

quizData.question: A comment should describe each line of code in detail.
quizData.explanation: Comments should explain the purpose and reasoning, not restate the obvious. Too many comments can clutter code.

slides.title: Use ShellCheck & Linting 🔍
slides.content:
## Automate Quality

`shellcheck` is a static analysis tool that catches dozens of common mistakes and style violations.

- Install: `apt install shellcheck` or `brew install shellcheck`.
- Run: `shellcheck myscript.sh`.
- Integrate with your editor (VS Code, Vim, etc.).

Make it a habit to lint every script before committing.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content: Version control (Git) is essential. Write a `.gitignore` that excludes temporary files, and commit only your source scripts and test data.
